stem: A newborn boy develops skin blisters at sites of minor friction. Electron microscopy of a skin biopsy shows absent anchoring fibrils at the dermal-epidermal junction.
oneliner: Newborn M + blisters at friction sites + EM: absent anchoring fibrils → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Desmoglein autoantibodies** in adults; the defect here is structural, not autoimmune
whyNot.B: **Autoimmune** disease of older adults against hemidesmosomes, not an inherited fibril defect
whyNot.D: **Collagen defect causes skin hyperextensibility and joint laxity**, not friction blisters
whyNot.E: **Blisters then swirled pigment** in a girl; the fibril defect points elsewhere

why: **Blisters from minor friction** in a newborn with **absent anchoring fibrils** = epidermolysis bullosa.

stem: A 3-week-old girl has linear crops of vesicles and blisters on her arms and legs that began in the first weeks of life. Over the next months the blisters become warty, and later swirled, streaky brown patches appear on her trunk. Her mother has patchy skin changes and has had two miscarriages, both of male fetuses. The family pedigree shows only affected females across three generations and no affected males.
oneliner: 3-wk F + linear vesicles → warty → swirled brown streaks + mother with male miscarriages + only females affected → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blisters at friction sites** with no swirled pigment; not X-linked dominant with male lethality
whyNot.C: **Atrophic linear streaks with fat herniation**, no blister-then-pigment sequence
whyNot.D: **Hypopigmented** swirls with no preceding blistering, usually sporadic
whyNot.E: **Mosaic, not inherited**; café-au-lait macules without a blistering stage

why: **Blisters → warts → swirled pigment** with **X-linked dominant, male-lethal** inheritance = incontinentia pigmenti.

stem: A 2-year-old boy with normal growth and a normal gait has blistering sunburns after short sun exposure and dense freckling of the face and arms, with rough keratoses.
oneliner: 2M + blistering sunburn after brief sun + dense freckling + keratoses → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Gait ataxia and telangiectasias** are absent; skin damage is the main problem
whyNot.B: **Pancytopenia and radial ray defects**, not photosensitive freckling
whyNot.C: **Lack of pigment** would not cause dense freckling
whyNot.E: **Growth failure, deafness and neurologic decline** are absent; freckling is not typical

why: **Early sun damage, freckling and keratoses** in a toddler = defective nucleotide excision repair (xeroderma pigmentosum).

stem: A 1-week-old boy is brought in for a skin lesion that has been present since birth. He is otherwise well. A photograph of the lesion is shown.
oneliner: 1-wk M + skin patch since birth + [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Raised, darker, often hairy** lesion; this patch is flat and uniform
whyNot.B: **Blue-gray** color; this patch is tan-brown
whyNot.C: **Red, raised** vascular lesion; this patch is not red
whyNot.D: **Bruise** with color changes and trauma history; this patch is uniform and stable

why: **Flat, uniform tan-brown patch** present at birth = café-au-lait spot.

image.prompt: A well-demarcated, flat, uniformly light tan-brown oval patch with smooth borders on the trunk skin of a newborn infant. No labels or text.

stem: A 4-month-old girl has a skin lesion on her cheek that first appeared at 2 months of age and has grown quickly since. She is otherwise healthy. A photograph of the lesion is shown.
oneliner: 4F + cheek lesion appeared at 2 mo + rapid growth + [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Present at birth, flat**, grows only with the child
whyNot.C: **Present at birth** and grows in proportion with the child, without a rapid growth phase
whyNot.D: **Single friable lesion** that bleeds easily, usually in older children
whyNot.E: **Small dome papule in adults**, not rapidly growing in an infant

why: **Appears after birth, grows fast, raised bright red** = infantile hemangioma (expected to involute).

image.prompt: A raised, bright red, lobulated soft nodule with a slightly glossy surface on the cheek of a 4-month-old infant. No labels or text.

stem: A 31-year-old woman who works as a dental hygienist has had an itchy, red, scaly rash with small vesicles on both hands for 2 weeks. The rash stops sharply at the wrist creases and gets worse 1 to 2 days after shifts with a new brand of gloves. She has never had hives, wheeze or facial swelling when putting on gloves. She has no personal or family history of eczema or asthma. A skin scraping with potassium hydroxide is negative. Patch testing is positive for a rubber additive.
oneliner: 31F + itchy vesicular rash on hands to the wrist + worse 1–2 d after shifts with new gloves + patch test positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Immediate** hives, wheeze or swelling within minutes; her rash is delayed
whyNot.B: **Burning, no positive patch test**; not immune-mediated
whyNot.D: **No atopic history** and rash is confined to the glove area
whyNot.E: **KOH negative**, so no fungal infection

why: **Delayed rash in the glove area** with a **positive patch test** = allergic contact dermatitis.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has intensely itchy linear streaks of red papules and vesicles on both forearms that began 2 days after she cleared brush on a hiking trail. She has no fever and no other medical problems.
oneliner: 19F + itchy linear streaks of red papules and vesicles on forearms 2 d after clearing brush → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Flexural chronic eczema** with atopic history; this is acute and linear after plant exposure
whyNot.C: **Wheals that fade within hours**; this rash has vesicles and appeared after 2 days
whyNot.D: **Burning, appears within hours** after a direct irritant; this one is itchy and delayed
whyNot.E: **Painful dermatomal band**, not bilateral linear itchy streaks

answer: Allergic contact dermatitis (poison ivy, type IV hypersensitivity)
why: **Linear vesicles 2 days after plant exposure** = T-cell mediated allergic contact dermatitis.

stem: A 24-year-old man has well-demarcated plaques with thick silvery scale on his elbows, knees and scalp that improve in summer sun.
oneliner: 24M + silvery-scaled plaques on elbows, knees, scalp + better with sunlight → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Greasy yellow scale** on the face and folds, not thick silvery plaques
whyNot.B: **Ill-defined weepy flexural patches**, not sharp extensor plaques
whyNot.C: **Annular with central clearing**, not thick silvery plaques
whyNot.E: **Purple, flat-topped itchy papules**, not silvery scale

why: **Sharp silvery plaques on extensor surfaces** that respond to UV light = plaque psoriasis.

stem: A 45-year-old man has sharply demarcated red plaques with thick silvery scale on both knees and elbows. When the scale is scraped off, pinpoint bleeding appears. He also reports morning stiffness and swelling in several distal finger joints.
oneliner: 45M + silvery plaques on knees and elbows + pinpoint bleeding when scraped + swollen distal finger joints → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Scarring, atrophic plaques with follicular plugging** on the face, no Auspitz sign
whyNot.B: **Violaceous flat-topped papules**, not scaly silvery plaques
whyNot.C: **Annular central clearing**; does not cause arthritis
whyNot.D: **Orange-red plaques with islands of sparing** and follicular papules, no arthritis

why: **Silvery plaques with Auspitz sign** and distal joint involvement = psoriasis.

stem: A 22-year-old woman who feels well has a mildly itchy eruption of oval, salmon-colored scaly patches on her trunk, aligned along the skin lines, that began 10 days after a single larger scaly patch appeared on her abdomen. Her palms and soles are spared.
oneliner: 22F + larger scaly abdominal patch → 10 d later oval salmon patches along skin lines on trunk + palms/soles spared → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Palm and sole involvement, systemic symptoms**; neither is present
whyNot.C: **Burrows in finger webs and intense nocturnal itch**, not trunk ovals
whyNot.D: **Bright red cheeks (slapped face)** with lacy limb rash
whyNot.E: **Dome-shaped umbilicated papules**, not scaly patches

why: **Herald patch followed by Christmas-tree trunk eruption** = pityriasis rosea.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has had many small, painless, non-itchy red bumps on the outer upper arms for 3 months. They feel rough like sandpaper and worry her only because of how they look. A photograph of the lesions is shown.
oneliner: 16F + painless nonitchy rough bumps on upper arms x 3 mo + [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pustules that are tender or itchy** around hairs; these bumps are dry, skin-colored to red, and painless
whyNot.C: **Itchy**, ill-defined eczematous patches in flexures, not discrete follicular papules
whyNot.D: **Painful nodules and sinus tracts in axillae and groin**, not rough arm papules
whyNot.E: **Transient itchy wheals**, not persistent follicular bumps

why: **Small, painless, follicular papules on the extensor arms** in an adolescent = keratosis pilaris.

image.prompt: Close view of the outer upper arm skin covered with many tiny, uniform, rough, skin-colored to pink follicular papules, each centered on a hair follicle, with no scale or pustules. No labels or text.

stem: A 14-year-old boy has blackheads, inflamed papules and pustules over his forehead and cheeks that began around the onset of puberty.
oneliner: 14M + blackheads + papules and pustules on face since puberty → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Flushing and redness in adults**, no blackheads
whyNot.B: **Uniform follicular pustules without comedones**
whyNot.D: **Confined to the mouth area, sparing the vermilion border**, no blackheads
whyNot.E: **Greasy yellow scale** on the eyebrows and nasolabial folds, no comedones or pustules

why: **Comedones with papules and pustules** starting at puberty = acne vulgaris (androgen-driven sebaceous activity).

stem: A 17-year-old boy wears a hard hat during his summer job. For 2 months he has had small pustules, papules and a few blackheads limited to the forehead under the helmet band. The skin is not itchy and the rest of his face is clear.
oneliner: 17M + hard hat worn daily + forehead-only papules, pustules and blackheads x 2 mo + not itchy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Itchy eczematous or vesicular** rash, no blackheads
whyNot.B: **Uniform follicular pustules** without blackheads
whyNot.C: **Greasy yellow scale** in the eyebrows and hairline, not comedones
whyNot.E: **Flushing and persistent redness** in adults, no blackheads

why: **Comedones with inflamed papules** limited to skin under friction and occlusion = acne vulgaris.

stem: A 17-year-old girl has had blackheads, inflamed papules, pustules and nodules on her face and upper back for 2 years. It improves on oral tetracycline but returns each time it is stopped.
oneliner: 17F + blackheads, papules, pustules and nodules on face and back x 2 y + relapses when oral antibiotic stopped → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Flushing and redness in older adults**, no blackheads
whyNot.C: **Pustules around hairs without blackheads or nodules**
whyNot.D: **Painful nodules in axillae and groin**, not face and back
whyNot.E: **Papules around the mouth** sparing the vermilion border, no blackheads

why: **Blackheads plus inflammatory papules and nodules** on face and back = chronic acne vulgaris.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has persistent redness of the nose and cheeks with scattered papules and pustules around the mouth. Hot drinks make her face flush. There are no blackheads, and she is distressed about her appearance.
oneliner: 42F + persistent redness over nose and cheeks + papules around mouth + flushes with hot drinks + no blackheads → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blackheads** are the hallmark and are absent here
whyNot.B: **Perioral rash sparing the vermilion border**, without central facial flushing
whyNot.C: **Greasy yellow scale** in nasolabial folds, no pustules or flushing
whyNot.D: **Malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds** with photosensitivity, not triggered flushing

why: **Central facial redness with papules and pustules, flushing, no comedones** = rosacea.

stem: A 22-year-old Black man has painful, itchy, hyperpigmented papules and pustules on his cheeks, jaw and neck. They worsen after daily close shaves, and he has no blackheads.
oneliner: 22M (Black) + painful itchy hyperpigmented papules on cheeks, jaw, neck + worse after close shaving + no blackheads → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blackheads** absent; bumps track with shaving
whyNot.C: **Firm scar-like growths beyond wound margins**, not papules from shaved hairs
whyNot.D: **Facial flushing and redness**, not hyperpigmented papules limited to beard area
whyNot.E: **Photosensitive scarring plaques**, not shave-related papules

why: **Beard-area papules after close shaving** from curved ingrown hairs = pseudofolliculitis barbae.

stem: A 74-year-old man has had itchy red patches on his abdomen and thighs for weeks, and now tense, large blisters have appeared on the thighs and forearms. Gentle pressure does not extend the blisters, and his mouth is spared. He takes no new medications.
oneliner: 74M + itchy red patches → tense large blisters on thighs and forearms + no spread with pressure + mouth spared + no new drugs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Flaccid blisters, oral erosions** and skin that slides with pressure
whyNot.B: **Small grouped itchy vesicles** on elbows, knees and buttocks with celiac disease, not large tense bullae
whyNot.C: **Mucosal erosions and widespread skin sloughing** after a drug trigger; no new drugs and mouth spared
whyNot.E: **Inherited disorder presenting in infancy**, not new tense blisters in an old man

why: **Tense blisters on itchy red skin in an elderly patient with the mouth spared** = bullous pemphigoid (linear IgG/C3 against hemidesmosomes).

stem: A 63-year-old man has painful erosions in his mouth and flaccid blisters on his scalp, face, groin and trunk that rupture easily. He takes no new medications. Pressure on normal skin next to a blister makes the top layer slide off. A biopsy shows an intraepidermal blister with loose, rounded keratinocytes just above the basal layer.
oneliner: 63M + painful oral erosions + flaccid blisters that rupture + skin slides with pressure + suprabasal acantholysis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Subepidermal** blister with tense bullae and no oral lesions
whyNot.B: **Itchy grouped vesicles on extensor surfaces** with a subepidermal split
whyNot.D: **Full-thickness epidermal necrosis** after a drug, not intraepidermal acantholysis
whyNot.E: **Superficial split in the granular layer** with crusted erosions and no mouth lesions

why: **Oral erosions, flaccid blisters, and suprabasal acantholysis** from anti-desmoglein antibodies = pemphigus vulgaris.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with celiac disease has intensely itchy grouped vesicles and crusted papules on her elbows, knees and buttocks.
oneliner: 38F + celiac disease + itchy grouped vesicles and crusts on elbows, knees, buttocks → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Large tense bullae in older adults**, not small grouped vesicles with celiac disease
whyNot.C: **Flaccid blisters and oral erosions**, not grouped itchy vesicles
whyNot.D: **Tense blisters at sites of trauma** that heal with scarring, not grouped itchy vesicles with celiac disease
whyNot.E: **Vesicles confined to palms, soles and sides of fingers**

why: **Itchy grouped vesicles on elbows, knees and buttocks** in a patient with **celiac disease** = dermatitis herpetiformis (granular IgA in dermal papillae).

stem: A 28-year-old woman develops a rash on her hands and forearms 10 days after starting amoxicillin for sinusitis. The lesions are round with a dusky center, a pale ring and an outer red ring, and a few have a central blister. There is no mucosal involvement, and under 5% of her skin is affected. Biopsy shows basal layer degeneration and keratinocyte necrosis with interface dermatitis.
oneliner: 28F + round lesions with dusky center, pale ring, red rim on hands/forearms 10 d after amoxicillin + no mucosal disease → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Mucosal erosions and skin sloughing** are absent; this has under 5% body surface
whyNot.C: **Wheals that come and go within 24 hours**, not fixed targets with interface change
whyNot.D: **Eczematous, geometric rash** at the contact site, not targets
whyNot.E: **Honey-crusted lesions** around the face, not targets

why: **Target lesions on the extremities with interface dermatitis**, no mucosal involvement = erythema multiforme.

stem: A 36-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a painful rash, burning eyes and mouth sores. Ten days ago she started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection. The rash began on her trunk as dusky red macules that merged and blistered. Gentle pressure on the skin makes the top layer slide off, and about 40% of her body surface is involved with erosions of the lips and conjunctivae. A biopsy shows full-thickness necrosis of the epidermis with very little inflammation in the dermis.
oneliner: 36F + painful blistering rash, mouth and eye erosions 10 d after TMP-SMX + skin slides off with pressure + >30% BSA + full-thickness epidermal necrosis → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Target lesions on the limbs with minimal mucosal disease and under 10% body surface**, not widespread sloughing
whyNot.B: **Toxin-mediated split high in the epidermis (granular layer)** in infants, with spared mucosa
whyNot.C: **Suprabasal acantholysis** and a chronic course, not drug-triggered full-thickness necrosis
whyNot.D: **Tense subepidermal blisters in a rosette (string of pearls) pattern** with linear IgA, not widespread necrosis

why: **Sulfa drug trigger, mucosal erosions, sloughing of >30% skin, full-thickness epidermal necrosis** = toxic epidermal necrolysis (SJS/TEN spectrum).

stem: A 35-year-old woman has a symmetric rash of small red macules and papules over her trunk and limbs that began 7 days after she started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a urinary infection. The rash is mildly itchy, and she has no fever, blisters or mouth sores. She recently got a new cat.
oneliner: 35F + symmetric red macules/papules on trunk and limbs 7 d into TMP-SMX + mild itch + no fever, blisters or mouth sores → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Eczematous rash at the sites of contact** with an allergen; she has no new contact exposure and the rash is diffuse and symmetric
whyNot.C: **Fever, hypotension and multi-organ involvement**; she is well
whyNot.D: **Annular scaly patches with central clearing**, not a symmetric, diffuse macular rash
whyNot.E: **Immediate sneezing, wheeze or hives**, not a delayed painless morbilliform rash

why: **Symmetric measles-like rash a week after starting a sulfa antibiotic**, without fever, blisters or mucosal sores = morbilliform drug eruption.

stem: A 20-year-old woman taking doxycycline for acne develops a painful, swollen, blistering red rash on her face, neck and forearms a few hours after an hour at the beach. The skin under her swimsuit is spared.
oneliner: 20F + painful blistering exaggerated sunburn within hours of 1 h beach + on doxycycline + only exposed skin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: One hour of sun would not usually blister skin this fast; the **doxycycline** explains the exaggerated burn
whyNot.B: **Delayed, itchy eczematous rash** needing prior sensitization
whyNot.D: **Itchy papules appearing 1 to 2 days after sun**, not painful blisters within hours
whyNot.E: **Joint pain and antinuclear antibodies** with a different drug history; no immediate blistering

why: **Exaggerated burn within hours** on exposed skin while taking a tetracycline = phototoxic drug reaction.

stem: A 2-year-old boy has had fever, irritability and tender red skin for 2 days. Large flaccid blisters have formed over his trunk and abdomen and rupture to leave moist red skin. His mouth and eyes are not involved, and he has no new medications. There are crusted lesions around his nose.
oneliner: 2M + fever + tender red skin + large flaccid bullae on trunk that rupture + mouth spared + crusting around nose → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **New drug and mucosal erosions**; here there is no drug and the mouth is spared
whyNot.C: **Localized blisters without fever or widespread tender skin**
whyNot.D: **Grouped painful vesicles on an erythematous base**, not large flaccid bullae
whyNot.E: **Lifelong blistering from friction since birth**, not an acute febrile illness

why: **Febrile toddler with tender skin and flaccid bullae, mucosa spared** from exfoliative toxin = staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome.

stem: A 33-year-old man has a painful, warm, fluctuant 3-cm swelling that drains pus at the site where a wood splinter entered his forearm 2 days ago.
oneliner: 33M + painful warm fluctuant swelling with pus at splinter site x 2 d → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Diffuse spreading redness without a pus collection**
whyNot.B: **Small superficial pustules around hair follicles**, not a deep 3-cm collection
whyNot.C: **Sharply raised, demarcated red plaque** on the face or legs, no fluctuance
whyNot.E: **Severe pain out of proportion, rapid spread and systemic toxicity**; this is localized and fluctuant

why: **Fluctuant, pus-filled painful swelling** at a puncture site = cutaneous abscess.

stem: A 19-year-old woman has itchy red papules and pustules over her trunk, buttocks and thighs that began 2 days after a party in a hot tub. Two friends who used the same tub have a similar rash.
oneliner: 19F + itchy follicular papules and pustules on trunk, buttocks, thighs 2 d after hot tub + friends affected → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Sporadic, in shaved or occluded sites** with no shared exposure
whyNot.B: **Blackheads and facial predominance**, not a shared water exposure
whyNot.C: **Burrows in finger webs and night itch**; spread by skin contact over weeks
whyNot.D: **Annular scaly patch with central clearing**, not diffuse follicular pustules

why: **Follicular pustules after hot tub exposure, with others affected** = Pseudomonas hot tub folliculitis.

stem: A 6-year-old boy has had many painless, mildly itchy skin lesions on his trunk and armpits for 2 months. He is otherwise healthy, and a classmate has similar lesions. A photograph of the lesions is shown.
oneliner: 6M + many painless mildly itchy lesions on trunk and axillae x 2 mo + classmate affected + [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Intense nocturnal itch with burrows**, not discrete papules
whyNot.C: **Annular scaly plaques** with central clearing, not dome-shaped papules
whyNot.D: **Beefy red moist patches with satellite pustules** in folds
whyNot.E: **Rough, hyperkeratotic papules** with black dots, not smooth dome-shaped papules

why: **Dome-shaped, centrally umbilicated papules** in a child = molluscum contagiosum (poxvirus).

image.prompt: Close view of a child's trunk and armpit skin with many small, smooth, pearly, skin-colored dome-shaped papules, each with a small central dimple (umbilication). No labels or text.

stem: A 27-year-old woman has a repeat Pap smear that shows atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance. She has no symptoms. Pelvic examination shows a normal-appearing cervix with no ulcers, warts, discharge or mass. Reflex testing for high-risk viral DNA is positive.
oneliner: 27F + repeat Pap with atypical squamous cells + no symptoms + normal cervix + high-risk viral DNA positive → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Invasive tumor on exam or biopsy** is absent; only atypical cells are seen
whyNot.B: **Painful vesicles or ulcers**; her cervix is normal
whyNot.D: **Cervicitis with discharge**, and it does not cause squamous atypia
whyNot.E: **Frothy discharge and a strawberry cervix**, not asymptomatic atypia

why: **Atypical squamous cells with positive high-risk viral DNA** = high-risk HPV infection (E6 degrades p53, E7 inactivates Rb).

stem: A 24-year-old man has noticed painless, non-itchy, fine-scaling patches on his back and shoulders that stay pale while the surrounding skin tans. He is otherwise well.
oneliner: 24M + painless nonitchy fine-scaling patches on back that stay pale while rest tans → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Itchy annular plaques with an active red border**, not fine-scaling pale macules
whyNot.B: **Fever, palm and sole rash, and lymphadenopathy**; he is well
whyNot.C: **Fully depigmented, non-scaly** patches
whyNot.E: **Herald patch and oval pink plaques along skin lines**; these are pale macules

why: **Nonitchy, scaly dyspigmented macules on the back** that stand out with tanning = tinea versicolor.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has had intense itching, worse at night, for 3 weeks. She has excoriated papules and thin gray lines in the finger webs, wrists, axillae and groin. Her younger brother has started to itch too.
oneliner: 7F + intense itch worse at night x 3 wk + papules and thin lines in finger webs, wrists, axillae, groin + brother itching → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Flexural eczema with personal atopy**, no burrows and no household spread
whyNot.C: **Rash matches a single exposed contact site**, no burrows
whyNot.D: **Scattered papules on exposed skin** from a single event, not shared and not burrowing
whyNot.E: **Linear groups of bites on exposed skin** without burrows in web spaces

why: **Nocturnal itch, burrows in web spaces and folds, household spread** = scabies.

stem: An 8-year-old girl has had an intensely itchy scalp for 2 weeks, and two classmates have the same problem. Small white oval particles are firmly stuck to the hair shafts near the scalp and do not brush off.
oneliner: 8F + intensely itchy scalp + classmates affected + white oval particles stuck to hair shafts → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Scaly patches with broken hairs**; nothing cemented to the hair shaft
whyNot.B: **Burrows in the finger webs and body folds**, not the scalp
whyNot.D: **Greasy flaking scale** that brushes off, no cemented particles
whyNot.E: **Chronic flexural eczema** with personal atopy, no outbreak

why: **Itchy scalp, classroom outbreak, nits cemented to hair shafts** = head lice.

stem: A 41-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after escaping a house fire. His chest, abdomen and both arms have blistered and charred skin, covering about 40% of his body surface. His voice is normal, there is no soot in his airway, and his carboxyhemoglobin is normal. Blood cultures are negative.
oneliner: 41M + house fire + blistered and charred skin over chest, abdomen, both arms (40% BSA) + normal voice, no soot in airway, normal COHb, cultures negative → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Soot in airway, hoarse voice, high carboxyhemoglobin** are absent
whyNot.C: **Positive cultures and an infectious source** are absent
whyNot.D: **Drug trigger and skin that slides with light pressure**, not charred skin after a fire
whyNot.E: **Hot dry skin and confusion with a core temperature above 40 C**, not skin destruction

why: **Skin destruction over 40% of the body after a fire** = major burn injury.

stem: A 30-year-old man grasps a hot pan handle. Within 20 minutes the palm is red and painful, with a fluid-filled blister at the site.
oneliner: 30M + grabs hot pan handle + red painful palm and blister within 20 min → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Delayed over days** after an allergen; this rash appears in minutes
whyNot.C: **Spreading warmth and fever over days** after bacterial entry, not a blister within minutes
whyNot.D: **Tense blisters in older adults** that appear over weeks with itch
whyNot.E: **Grouped vesicles on an erythematous base** with prodromal tingling, not a single blister after heat

why: **Blister and redness minutes after touching a hot object** = partial-thickness burn with early histamine-driven vascular leak.

stem: A 16-year-old boy collapses while mowing lawns on a hot summer day. At age 5 he had burns over most of his trunk and legs that were treated with skin grafts. His temperature is 41.5 C (106.7 F), he is confused, and his skin is hot and dry over the grafted areas. He takes no medications.
oneliner: 16M + collapse mowing in summer heat + childhood burns with skin grafts + T 41.5 C, confused, hot dry skin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Temperature below 40 C with normal mentation**, not confusion
whyNot.B: **Needs a volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine trigger**, none given
whyNot.C: **Needs an antipsychotic and rigidity**, he takes no medications
whyNot.E: **Needs goiter, tremor and hyperthyroid history** with tachyarrhythmia, not environmental heat exposure

why: **Core temperature above 40 C with confusion after heat exposure, scarred skin without sweat glands** = heat stroke.

stem: A 52-year-old man with long-standing paraplegia and no diabetes is admitted for a urinary tract infection. On hospital day 5 he has a shallow ulcer over his sacrum with surrounding red skin that does not blanch.
oneliner: 52M + long-standing paraplegia + no diabetes + sacral ulcer with nonblanching surrounding erythema → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Medial ankle ulcer with edema and hyperpigmentation**, not over a bony prominence
whyNot.B: **Painful, punched-out toe ulcer with absent pulses**, not sacral
whyNot.C: **Plantar ulcer in a diabetic with neuropathy**, he is not diabetic
whyNot.D: **Rapidly expanding violaceous ulcer** with inflammatory bowel disease, not over a pressure point

why: **Ulcer over a bony prominence in an immobile patient** = pressure ulcer.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has a raised, firm, itchy scar that has grown beyond the margins of her sternotomy incision over 3 months.
oneliner: 25F + 3 mo after sternotomy + raised firm scar growing beyond the incision margins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Stays within the original wound margins**, and may regress
whyNot.C: **Soft, moist, red tissue** in an open healing wound, not a firm closed scar
whyNot.D: **Small firm brown nodule** with dimple sign, not at an incision
whyNot.E: **Slowly growing plaque without prior surgery**, not a scar beyond an incision

why: **Scar tissue that grows beyond the wound margins** from excess collagen = keloid.

stem: A 9-year-old girl has a small, slightly tender nodule on her chin, at the site where a laceration was repaired with sutures 10 weeks ago. A biopsy shows epithelioid histiocytes and multinucleated giant cells surrounding fragments of refractile material.
oneliner: 9F + tender chin nodule at laceration repair site 10 wk ago + giant cells and histiocytes around refractile material → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Dense, thick collagen bundles** extending beyond the scar, not granulomas
whyNot.C: **Neutrophils, pus and fever**, not epithelioid histiocytes
whyNot.D: **Cyst lined by epithelium with skin appendages**, present since birth
whyNot.E: **Non-caseating granulomas without foreign material**, with systemic findings

why: **Nodule at a repair site with giant cells around refractile suture material** = foreign body granuloma.

stem: An 81-year-old woman has recurrent large, flat purple bruises on the backs of her forearms and hands. The skin there is thin, wrinkled and sun-damaged with brown macules. She recalls no trauma, has no injuries elsewhere, and has no mucosal bleeding. Platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal.
oneliner: 81F + recurrent large flat purple bruises on sun-damaged forearms and hands + no trauma, no mucosal bleeding + normal platelets, PT, aPTT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **PT and aPTT are normal**; bruising is limited to sun-damaged skin
whyNot.B: **Injuries in varied sites** with inconsistent history; hers are only on sun-exposed extensor skin
whyNot.C: **Platelet count is normal** and petechiae and mucosal bleeding are absent
whyNot.E: **Small telangiectasias on lips and nosebleeds** in a family history, not flat purpura

why: **Large bruises limited to sun-damaged forearms with normal clotting tests** = senile purpura.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has fine wrinkles, mottled brown pigmentation and a leathery texture on her face and neck. The skin on her buttocks is smooth. She spent many summers sunbathing.
oneliner: 52F + fine wrinkles, mottled pigment, leathery face and neck + smooth buttock skin + years of sunbathing → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Discrete rough scaly premalignant papules**, not diffuse wrinkling
whyNot.B: **Comedones and pustules**, not wrinkles
whyNot.D: **Discrete flat brown macules**, not diffuse wrinkling and leathery texture
whyNot.E: **Stuck-on waxy brown plaques**, not fine wrinkles

why: **Wrinkled, mottled, leathery skin only where sun-exposed** = photoaging.

stem: A 30-year-old man has thinning hair over the crown with a receding frontal hairline. His father became bald in his thirties. The scalp skin looks normal, with no scaling or patches of complete hair loss.
oneliner: 30M + thinning at crown and receding hairline + father bald + normal scalp skin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Sharp round patches of complete hair loss**, not diffuse thinning
whyNot.B: **Diffuse shedding after a stressful event** with no frontal recession
whyNot.C: **Scaly patches with broken hairs**, scalp here is normal
whyNot.D: **Irregularly broken hairs from pulling**, not patterned thinning

why: **Patterned crown and frontal thinning with family history and normal scalp** = androgenetic alopecia.

stem: A 72-year-old farmer has had rough, sandpaper-like, scaly red plaques on his scalp, ears and forearms for years. They are not itchy, but picking at them causes slight bleeding. He has worked outdoors without a hat all his life.
oneliner: 72M + outdoor farmer + rough scaly red plaques on scalp, ears, forearms for years + not itchy → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Nodule that is indurated, ulcerated or rapidly growing**; these plaques are flat and stable
whyNot.B: **Stuck-on waxy plaques** with a greasy surface, not rough sandpaper scale
whyNot.D: **Silvery scale on elbows and knees**, not sun-exposed skin only
whyNot.E: **Pearly nodule with telangiectasias**, not scaly plaques

why: **Rough scaly plaques on chronically sun-exposed skin** = actinic keratosis.

stem: A 68-year-old man who golfs often has a slowly growing pearly, translucent nodule with fine surface vessels on his nose.
oneliner: 68M + golfer + slowly growing pearly translucent nodule on nose + telangiectasias → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Pigmented, irregular lesion**; this nodule is pearly and not pigmented
whyNot.C: **Rough scaly flat lesion**, not a pearly nodule
whyNot.D: **Waxy stuck-on brown plaque**, not a pearly translucent nodule
whyNot.E: **Scaly, keratotic or ulcerated nodule**, not pearly with telangiectasias

why: **Pearly translucent nodule with telangiectasias** on sun-exposed skin = basal cell carcinoma (palisading basaloid nests on biopsy).

dx: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
stem: A 70-year-old fair-skinned man has an ulcerated, firm nodule on his cheek that has grown steadily for 8 months. He has had decades of heavy sun exposure. A biopsy shows invasive atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls.
oneliner: 70M + fair skin + decades of sun + ulcerated firm cheek nodule growing for 8 mo + invasive squamous cells with keratin pearls → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin

whyNot.A: **Palisading basaloid nests with clefting**, not keratin pearls
whyNot.B: **Atypical melanocytes with pigment**, not squamous cells
whyNot.C: **Atypia confined to the epidermis** without invasion
whyNot.E: **Rapid growth over weeks, central keratin plug, then regresses**; this one grew slowly and ulcerated

answer: Squamous cell carcinoma of the skin
why: **Ulcerated nodule on sun-damaged skin with invasive keratinizing squamous cells** = cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.

stem: A 54-year-old woman has a pigmented lesion on her forearm that has grown and changed color over 6 months. It is now over 6 mm across. A photograph of the lesion is shown.
oneliner: 54F + forearm pigmented lesion enlarging and changing color x 6 mo + >6 mm + [photo] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pearly translucent nodule with telangiectasias**, not variegated pigment
whyNot.B: Usually **stable over time**; this lesion is **growing and changing color**
whyNot.C: **Stuck-on waxy surface** with a uniform color, not asymmetric and variegated
whyNot.D: **Symmetric, round and uniformly colored**, not irregular and changing

why: **Asymmetric, multicolored, enlarging lesion over 6 mm** = melanoma.

image.prompt: A pigmented lesion on a woman's forearm that is asymmetric with irregular, notched borders and mixed shades of black, brown and tan, slightly raised in part, about 8 mm across. No labels or text.

stem: A 69-year-old woman has had a 1-cm lesion on her nostril that has bled intermittently for 1 month. A biopsy shows sheets of atypical cells with abundant coarse brown granular pigment in the cytoplasm.
oneliner: 69F + 1-cm bleeding nostril lesion x 1 mo + biopsy: sheets of atypical cells packed with brown granular pigment → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Basaloid nests with palisading and clefts**, not pigment-laden cells
whyNot.C: **Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges**, not pigmented cells
whyNot.D: **Atypical keratinocytes confined to the epidermis**, no pigment
whyNot.E: **Cross-striated spindle or round cells** with desmin, no pigment granules

why: **Tumor cells packed with melanin granules** = melanoma.

stem: A 58-year-old Black man has a growing dark brown-black patch with irregular borders and a bleeding center on the sole of his foot. He recalls no injury there.
oneliner: 58M (Black) + growing dark irregular patch with bleeding center on the sole + no injury → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Pearly nodule on sun-exposed skin**, rare on the sole
whyNot.B: **Scaly ulcerated nodule on sun-damaged skin**, not dark irregular pigment
whyNot.D: **Rough keratotic papule with black dots** (thrombosed vessels), not a spreading dark patch
whyNot.E: **Flat, painless brown-black macule on the palm in tropical regions**, not a growing patch with bleeding

why: **Growing irregular dark lesion on the sole of a dark-skinned patient** = acral lentiginous melanoma.

stem: A 78-year-old woman has a flat brown-black patch on her cheek that has enlarged slowly over 8 years. It has mottled color and irregular borders. A biopsy shows atypical melanocytes along the basal layer of sun-damaged epidermis, with no invasion.
oneliner: 78F + enlarging irregular mottled brown-black facial patch x 8 y + atypical melanocytes along basal layer, no invasion → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Atypical keratinocytes** and scaly surface, not atypical melanocytes
whyNot.C: **Stuck-on waxy plaque** with horn cysts, not a flat patch with basal atypical melanocytes
whyNot.D: **Symmetric, stable** lesion with nests of benign melanocytes
whyNot.E: **Velvety hyperpigmentation in neck and axillary folds**, not a single facial patch

why: **Slowly growing irregular facial macule with atypical melanocytes along the basal layer** = lentigo maligna (melanoma in situ).

dx: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome
stem: A 34-year-old woman has more than 60 moles, many larger than 5 mm with irregular borders, on both sun-exposed skin and on her buttocks and scalp. Her father and two paternal aunts died of melanoma, and her paternal uncle died of pancreatic cancer.
oneliner: 34F + >60 large irregular moles incl. buttocks and scalp + father and two aunts died of melanoma + uncle with pancreatic cancer → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome

whyNot.A: **Single blue-gray benign nodule**, not numerous irregular moles
whyNot.B: **Stuck-on waxy plaques** in older adults without melanoma family history
whyNot.C: **Pearly nodule** on sun-exposed skin; does not explain multiple atypical moles
whyNot.E: **Pigmented lip and buccal macules with polyps**, not atypical moles

answer: Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome (CDKN2A)
why: **Numerous atypical moles with a strong family history of melanoma and pancreatic cancer** = FAMMM syndrome.
